before.label: Memory studies
before.description: Studies remembering, commemoration and forgetting through social relations, narratives, bodies and cultural forms. Recollection is evidence requiring interpretation; memory and history are connected in different, contested ways.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Maurice Halbwachs (1925) as a precursor; Pierre Nora, Les Lieux de mémoire (1984–92).

representative_people.context: Social frameworks make remembering a relational process; later English selections are distinct from the original French works. The original French conclusion also addresses changes in traditions through relations between groups.
representative_people.works: Les cadres sociaux de la mémoire (1925); On Collective Memory, ed. and trans. Lewis Coser (1992 selections)

representative_people.context: Studies sites where remembrance and historical reconstruction interact; his memory/history distinction is a situated argument.
representative_people.works: Les Lieux de mémoire (1984–92); “Between Memory and History” (English 1989)

representative_people.context: Brings habitual bodily practices into the study of social remembering.
Distinguishes everyday communication from institutionally maintained cultural memory while acknowledging collaboration with Aleida Assmann.
Studies the media and uses of cultural remembering; her contribution is visible beside their collaborative work.
Examines mourning after the Great War and questions a clean break between older and modern cultural forms.
representative_people.works: Sites of Memory, Sites of Mourning (1995)

representative_people.context: Examines Holocaust memorials and museums as historically situated forms of remembrance. A 1994 adapted extract examines memorial production, political disagreement and public participation.
Treats popular historical practices as part of the production of historical knowledge.
Interprets recollections of daily life under fascism without equating memory with either transparent evidence or resistance.
Brings feminist questions of subjectivity and the unconscious into historical work.
Mnemonic techniques and their historical transformations provide a comparison with social frameworks and commemoration, without a founding claim.
representative_people.works: The Art of Memory (1966), preface and concluding chapter

representative_people.context: Studies archival access and historical authority; Derrida explicitly credits her investigation. Included as an archival-history interlocutor, without identifying archives with all collective memory.
representative_people.works: Archives interdites: les peurs françaises face à l’histoire contemporaine (1994), as cited in Archive Fever, p. 4 note 1

representative_people.context: Examines institutions, inscription and preservation/destruction while distinguishing an archive from spontaneous recollection. A conceptual contribution, not proof that all memory historians adopted it.
representative_people.works: Archive Fever (lecture 1994; English book 1996), opening and selected exergue

representative_people.context: Connects public memory with urban landscapes through collaborative historical work.

before.scope_note: Halbwachs’s social frameworks, Nora’s commemorative sites, and Samuel’s popular uses of the past are distinct projects. Communicative and cultural memory are the Assmann project’s distinctions, not a universal taxonomy. War mourning, Holocaust memorials and feminist subjectivity require different historical explanations; this selection remains weighted toward European debates.

strands.title: Social frameworks of remembering
strands.focus: Family, religious and class contexts organize recollection; a collective framework is not proof of one identical group memory.
strands.works: Les cadres sociaux de la mémoire (1925); English selections (1992)

strands.title: Sites of memory and historical reconstruction
strands.focus: Sites combine material, symbolic and functional dimensions, extending beyond monuments alone.

strands.title: Habit, bodies and ceremony
strands.focus: Remembering includes bodily competence, not only recalled propositions or pictures.

strands.title: Communication and cultural objectivation
strands.focus: Everyday recollection and durable cultural forms operate differently; Assmann revises rather than merely repeats Halbwachs.

strands.title: Media and uses of cultural memory
strands.focus: Writing, images and monuments organize what can be stored and recalled.

strands.title: Mourning and cultural continuities after war
strands.focus: Traditional and modern forms overlap in Great War mourning; this is not a template for every subsequent catastrophe.
strands.works: Sites of Memory, Sites of Mourning (1995)

strands.title: Holocaust memorials and their contexts
strands.focus: Memorial forms and meanings vary across places and institutions.

strands.title: Popular practices of historical knowledge
strands.focus: Family research, images and reenactment make historical work visible outside professional writing.

strands.title: Life histories, gender and subjectivity
strands.focus: Fascist everyday life and feminist psychoanalytic inquiry are distinct routes into interpreted recollection.

strands.title: Archival authority, access and inscription
strands.focus: Combe’s inquiry into access supplies a named resource to Derrida. His account differentiates archives from spontaneous memory and examines institutional authority and technical inscription.

strands.title: Urban landscapes and public memory
strands.focus: Hayden’s collaborative practice links historical interpretation to lived places.

strands.title: Traditions in contact and conflict
strands.focus: Halbwachs explains revisions of collective remembering through contact with other groups and their traditions; social frameworks are not an assurance of a unanimous or unchanging past.
strands.works: Les cadres sociaux de la mémoire (1925), final concluding subsection

strands.title: Memorial production and public disagreement
strands.focus: Young’s Saarbrücken account follows a covert art project into public controversy and political recognition. His interpretation makes the memorial’s production and reception part of its meaning.
strands.works: Germany’s vanishing Holocaust monuments (1994), adapted extract

strands.title: Argentina: rights, remembrance and generations
strands.focus: Jelin examines competing public memories and tensions within human-rights activism. Her conclusion questions both political forgetting and repetition that prevents younger generations from reinterpreting the past.
strands.works: The Politics of Memory (1994), selected sections

strands.title: Vichy’s afterlife and historical inquiry
strands.focus: Rousso distinguishes memory as an object of research, as a preliminary examination of inherited representations, and as a way to extend an event’s historical study into its aftermath.
strands.works: Pour une histoire de la mémoire collective (1991), 163–166

strands.title: Jewish remembrance and historiography
strands.focus: Yerushalmi’s prologue asks why concern with historical meaning and remembrance need not give professional historical writing the central role. This is a situated historical question, not a timeless definition of Jewish people.

strands.title: Resources for studying forgetting
strands.focus: Jelin’s 1994 analysis explicitly draws on Yerushalmi’s transmission argument and Loraux’s treatment of amnesty and mourning. Their Spanish 1989 essays are distinct from Zakhor.
strands.works: Usos del olvido essays (1989), as used by Jelin (1994)

added.title: Elizabeth Jelin, “The Politics of Memory: The Human Rights Movement and the Construction of Democracy in Argentina,” Latin American Perspectives 21/2 (1994), 38–58.
added.citation: Elizabeth Jelin, “The Politics of Memory: The Human Rights Movement and the Construction of Democracy in Argentina,” Latin American Perspectives 21/2 (1994), 38–58.

verification.note: Read opening 38–40, complete “Memory, Truth, and Justice” section 46–52 and conclusion 52–53, notes 8–21 and selected references in a public PDF at https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?doi=0ec22d7e72d056057c62274abfb8b19dc4e26063&repid=rep1&type=pdf . Intervening 41–46 not fully read. Author credit names CEDES project and Pablo Azcárate’s participation. Yerushalmi and Loraux are cited resources, not independently read here; interviews not independently checked. This is the 1994 analysis, not subsequent legal outcomes or evidence that remembering guarantees non-recurrence.

No scan collation or detailed check of his periodization.

added.citation: Yosef Hayim Yerushalmi, Zakhor: Jewish History and Jewish Memory (1982; later editions).

verification.note: Publisher contents and 1996 edition checked; University of Washington finding-aid indexed entry separately records 1982/1996 copyright (https://static.lib.uw.edu/static/public/specialcollections/findingaids/02-019.pdf). Read legible prologue passages and selected opening-chapter lines in garbled public OCR at https://www.scribd.com/document/1010391836/Vdoc-pub-Zakhor-Jewish-History-and-Jewish-Memory . Supports only the stated distinction between historical meaning, remembering and historiography. No complete chapter, reliable scan collation, or reconstruction of missing OCR. Later prefaces not backdated; book-wide historical generalizations not adopted.

outcomes.finding: Added a researched pre-2000 Argentina project, distinguished Rousso and Yerushalmi, and recorded named collaboration and specific conceptual resources with bounded evidence.
outcomes.research_limit: Jelin 1994: opening 38–40, complete Memory/Truth/Justice section 46–52 and conclusion 52–53, notes 8–21 and selected references read; intervening body incomplete. Original interviews and cited Yerushalmi/Loraux essays not independently checked. Rousso 1991: public page OCR 163–166, including three methodological cases; later pages and book unread. Yerushalmi: publisher contents/edition metadata and selected legible prologue/early chapter OCR read; transcription substantially garbled, no complete chapter or first-edition collation. UW finding-aid indexed entry supports 1982/1996 copyright distinction. No general claim about all Latin American or Jewish remembering, no contemporary legal extrapolation, and no identity between Zakhor and the 1989 essay Jelin cites.
